content: Eczema is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that often affects areas such as the folds of the elbows or knees. It is characterized by intense itching and a relapsing-remitting course. Up to one-third of individuals with eczema who test positive for house dust mite allergy report worsening of their eczema or respiratory symptoms when exposed to dust. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of various house dust mite reduction and avoidance strategies in the treatment of eczema. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to August 14, 2014. These databases included the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and the GREAT database. Additionally, five trial registries were searched, and references from included and excluded studies were reviewed. Abstracts from international eczema and allergy conferences were also hand-searched. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of any age who were clinically diagnosed with eczema, as defined by the World Allergy Organization. Both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions aimed at reducing or avoiding exposure to house dust mites and their allergenic feces were considered. Comparators included active treatments, no treatment, placebo, or standard care. Two authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of identified studies, with no disagreements reported. Authors of included studies were contacted for additional information, and the risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane methodology. Seven studies involving a total of 324 participants (adults and children) were included. Overall, the studies were found to have a high risk of bias. Four of the studies tested interventions with multiple components, while three tested single interventions. Two studies included only children, four included both children and adults, and one included only adults. Interventions included the use of allergen-impermeable mattress and bedding covers, high-quality vacuuming of carpets and mattresses, and acaricide sprays. Four studies assessed the primary outcome of clinician-assessed eczema severity using a named scale. One study (n = 20) found no significant short-term benefit from allergen-impermeable polyurethane mattress encasings and acaricide spray compared to allergen-permeable cotton encasings and placebo spray. Another study (n = 60) reported a modest but statistically significant improvement in the Six Area, Six Sign Atopic Dermatitis (SASSAD) scale over six months (mean difference of 4.2, 95% CI 1.7 to 6.7, P = 0.008) in favor of a mite-impermeable bedding system combined with benzyltannate spray and high-filtration vacuuming versus mite-permeable cotton encasings, water with trace alcohol spray, and a low-filtration vacuum cleaner. A third study (n = 41) did not compare changes in eczema severity between treatment groups, and a fourth study (n = 86) found no evidence of a difference between groups. For secondary outcomes, one study (n = 20) assessed participantor caregiver-reported global eczema severity and the amount and frequency of topical treatment required, with similar results reported in both groups. Four studies (n = 159) evaluated sensitivity to house dust mite allergens using a marker, but no clear differences in sensitivity levels were observed between treatments. None of the studies assessed the second primary outcome of participantor caregiver-reported eczema-related quality of life using a named instrument, nor did they evaluate adverse effects. Due to variability in interventions and limited data, the results could not be combined. The authors concluded that the available evidence is of very low quality and does not provide clear guidance for clinical practice. The modest treatment responses observed were specific to individuals with atopic eczema and sensitivity to aeroallergens, leaving their applicability to the broader eczema population uncertain. High-quality, long-term trials focusing on single, easy-to-implement house dust mite reduction or avoidance measures are recommended for future research.
